sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduction explaining product master data versus transactional data and why consistent product identification matters across supply chain partners, then situating the handbook within the Digital implementation investment guide (DIIG), WHO SMART Guidelines (layers L1 to L5) and the digital health supply chain architecture's product registry; it also outlines the chapters, how the handbook was developed, target users per chapter, and when to use it.

narratives.en: Fig. 1, 'Product master data'. A health product, drawn as a boxed medicine package, is linked to PRODUCT MASTER DATA, shown as four categories with examples. General Information: product identifier, name, description, unit of measure. Classification: ICD, ATC, product characteristics/specifications. Pharmaceutical Information: dosage, strength, route of administration, doses per vial. Logistical Information: packaging, volumetrics, shelf life, storage temperature.

Fig. 2, 'Importance of product master data'. Three columns. On the left, SUPPLY CHAIN PARTNERS: manufacturers, procurers, Ministry of Health / programmes, donors, shippers, regulatory authority, central/regional/district warehouses and health facilities. On the right, SUPPLY CHAIN PROCESSES: forecasting and supply planning, procurement, ordering/re-ordering, inventory management, distribution, dispensing, product recalls and finance/insurance. Arrows from both point into the central PRODUCT MASTER DATA column — general information, classification details, pharmaceutical information, logistical information and other information — which flows down through a medicine icon to Patients.

Fig. 3, 'Impact of inconsistent product information'. An arrow labelled PHYSICAL FLOW OF HEALTH PRODUCTS runs across five actors: manufacturers, central warehouse, health facilities, community health workers and patients. Beneath them sit the systems each stage uses — a warehouse management system, an eLMIS and paper forms — and each holds the same product under a different code (123123, A1232, P44545, AM545). Broken-chain icons join the codes, showing that the identifiers do not link up along the chain.

Fig. 4, 'Planning and implementing a digital health enterprise: phases, steps and resources'. Seven numbered phases — assessing the current state and enabling environment; establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; defining the future state; planning the enterprise architecture; determining health content requirements; M&E and fostering data use; and implementing, maintaining and scaling — each with its steps. Resource tiles are placed against the phases they serve and marked as PDF or online, among them the DIIG, the WHO SMART guidelines with digital adaptation kits, TOGAF, OpenHIE and the WHO handbook for health supply chain architecture. The tile 'WHO handbook for health product catalogue (this document)' is highlighted in phase 07. It is the same chart as Fig. 6 of the WHO handbook for digitalizing primary health care, re-pointed to this document.

Fig. 5, 'WHO SMART Guidelines Approach'. A research and evidence base feeds five knowledge layers and their products: L1 Narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 Operational (digital adaptation kits), L3 Machine readable (machine-readable recommendations), L4 Executable (reference software) and L5 Dynamic (precision health models). Each passes through LOCALISATION into a country-implementation adaptation: national policies and procedures, localised requirements, localised machine-readable code and standards, localised static digital services, and dynamic applications optimised for local outcomes. All feed DATA, EVIDENCE, AND IMPACT, which returns to the evidence base as EVIDENCE FROM DIGITAL IMPLEMENTATIONS.

Fig. 6, 'Example of an Antenatal Care Business clinical workflow with highlighted' activities. The upper part is a swimlane process in a health facility, with Client and Health worker lanes. The client arrives at the facility, then goes through registration, rapid assessment and management, a danger-signs/referral decision, pregnancy confirmation, a first-contact decision and a quick check. These lead to collecting the woman's profile and history, then an ANC assessment (check symptoms and follow-up, conduct physical exam, conduct laboratory tests and imaging), then 10. Counselling, in-facility management and treatment, with subactivities 10.1 to 10.9, then a referral decision, scheduling, and self-care in the home or community until the woman returns. The lower part enlarges activities 6 to 10. Highlighted borders mark 9 (conduct laboratory tests and imaging), 10.5 nutrition supplementation, 10.7 immunizations and 10.9 deworming and malaria counselling and prophylaxis — the activities that involve health products.

Fig. 7, 'Digital health supply chain architecture framework'. Top row: SHARED SERVICES, whose foundational components are facility, product (highlighted) and supplier registries; DATA SERVICES, with analytics (supply chain reports, data warehouse) and traceability (track and trace, product verification); and Digital Ecosystems (quality, health management information, regulatory, and finance and insurance systems). A middle INTEROPERABILITY LAYER of enabling components: authentication, encryption, transformation, orchestration, validation and translation. Bottom: HEALTH SUPPLY CHAIN INFORMATION SYSTEMS — forecasting and planning, order management, warehouse management, cold chain management, procurement, supplier and contract management, transportation management and dispensing — beside External systems (global platforms, manufacturer systems, data repositories).

Fig. 8, 'Linkage across classifications, generic products and trade items'. Three columns: CLASSIFICATION (classes or groups of diseases, pathogens or drugs); PRODUCT (name/INN, strength, dosage form, route of administration); and TRADE ITEM (unique identifier such as a GTIN, brand name, manufacturer, country of origin, packaging details, volumetrics, shelf life). The example row traces Nervous system → Analgesics → Other analgesics and antipyretics → Anilides → Paracetamol to the product 'Paracetamol 500 mg tablet'. That product branches into two manufacturers' trade items, each with its own unique IDs and pack hierarchy: a case and inner pack of 100 from ABC Manufacturing (brand Ceta123), and a case, inner pack of 50 and each of 10 from XYZ Manufacturing (brand ParaXYZ). A bottom row gives each column's use: strategic (data aggregation and analysis), tactical (forecasting, procurement planning and aggregate visibility) and operational (inventory, distribution, tracking and tracing, pharmacovigilance and AEFI analysis).

Fig. 9, 'Relationship between generic product, trade item and regulated trade item'. Three classes are drawn as boxes listing their attributes with cardinalities. GENERIC PRODUCT has identifier 0..*, status, name (nameType, nameValue), description, classification, unitOfUse, dosageForm, strength, routeOfAdministration, manufacturer, countryOfOrigin, shelfLife, doseQuantity, attribute (type, value[x]) and associatedProduct (product, relationship, quantity). TRADE ITEM has identifier 1..*, status, tradeItemName, description, classification, manufacturer, countryOfOrigin, shelfLife, associatedGenericProduct (genericProduct, quantity), contains (tradeItem, quantity) and attribute. REGULATED TRADE ITEM has identifier, status, jurisdiction, authorisationHolder, validityPeriod, authorisedTradeItem, attribute and associatedProduct. The associations read: one generic product to zero or more trade items, and one trade item to zero or more regulated trade items.

Fig. 10, 'Product packaging hierarchy' (source: GS1.org), in the section on instituting data management and governance policies. It is drawn as a staircase of four grey steps, each holding packaging illustrations. The top step, labelled PRIMARY, shows individual items such as vials, a bottle, syringes in blister packs, a blister strip and a sterile-packed instrument. The next step, SECONDARY, shows boxes and cartons holding those items; the third, SECONDARY OR TERTIARY, shows open cartons and a row of boxed packs; and the bottom step, TERTIARY, shows shipping cases and a shrink-wrapped pallet of boxes.
narratives.fr: Fig. 10, « Hiérarchie des emballages de produits » (Product packaging hierarchy, source : GS1.org), dans la section consacrée à l'instauration de politiques de gestion et de gouvernance des données. Elle est représentée sous la forme d'un escalier à quatre marches grises portant chacune des illustrations d'emballages. La marche supérieure, intitulée PRIMAIRE (PRIMARY), montre des articles individuels tels que des flacons, une bouteille, des seringues sous blister, une plaquette thermoformée et un instrument sous emballage stérile. La marche suivante, SECONDAIRE (SECONDARY), montre des boîtes et des cartons contenant ces articles ; la troisième, SECONDAIRE OU TERTIAIRE (SECONDARY OR TERTIARY), montre des cartons ouverts et une rangée de boîtes conditionnées ; et la marche inférieure, TERTIAIRE (TERTIARY), montre des caisses d'expédition et une palette de boîtes filmée.
narratives.es: Fig. 10, «Jerarquía de embalaje de productos» (Product packaging hierarchy, fuente: GS1.org), en la sección sobre el establecimiento de políticas de gestión y gobernanza de datos. Está dibujada como una escalera de cuatro peldaños grises, cada uno con ilustraciones de envases y embalajes. El peldaño superior, etiquetado PRIMARIO (PRIMARY), muestra artículos individuales como viales, un frasco, jeringas en blísteres, una tira blíster y un instrumento en envase estéril. El siguiente peldaño, SECUNDARIO (SECONDARY), muestra cajas y estuches que contienen esos artículos; el tercero, SECUNDARIO O TERCIARIO (SECONDARY OR TERTIARY), muestra cajas abiertas y una fila de paquetes en cajas; y el peldaño inferior, TERCIARIO (TERTIARY), muestra cajas de envío y un palé de cajas envuelto en película retráctil.
narratives.ar: الشكل 10، «التسلسل الهرمي لتغليف المنتجات» (Product packaging hierarchy، المصدر: GS1.org)، في القسم الخاص بإرساء سياسات إدارة البيانات وحوكمتها. وقد رُسم على هيئة سلّم مكوّن من أربع درجات رمادية تحمل كل منها رسوماً توضيحية للتغليف. وتُظهر الدرجة العليا، المعنونة «الأولي» (PRIMARY)، مفردات فردية مثل القوارير، وزجاجة، ومحاقن في عبوات نفطية (بليستر)، وشريط بليستر، وأداة في غلاف معقم. وتُظهر الدرجة التالية، «الثانوي» (SECONDARY)، عُلباً وكراتين تحتوي على تلك المفردات؛ وتُظهر الدرجة الثالثة، «الثانوي أو الثالثي» (SECONDARY OR TERTIARY)، كراتين مفتوحة وصفاً من العبوات المعلبة؛ أما الدرجة السفلى، «الثالثي» (TERTIARY)، فتُظهر صناديق شحن ومنصة نقالة (طبلية) من الصناديق المغلفة بغشاء انكماشي.
narratives.ru: Рис. 10, «Иерархия упаковки продукции» (Product packaging hierarchy, источник: GS1.org), в разделе о внедрении политик управления данными и руководства ими. Диаграмма изображена в виде лестницы из четырех серых ступеней, на каждой из которых показаны иллюстрации упаковки. На верхней ступени с подписью ПЕРВИЧНАЯ (PRIMARY) показаны отдельные изделия: флаконы, бутылочка, шприцы в блистерных упаковках, блистерная пластина и стерильно упакованный инструмент. На следующей ступени — ВТОРИЧНАЯ (SECONDARY) — показаны коробки и пачки, содержащие эти изделия; на третьей — ВТОРИЧНАЯ ИЛИ ТРЕТИЧНАЯ (SECONDARY OR TERTIARY) — открытые картонные коробки и ряд упакованных коробок; а на нижней ступени — ТРЕТИЧНАЯ (TERTIARY) — транспортные ящики и обтянутый термоусадочной пленкой поддон с коробками.
narratives.zh: 图 10，“产品包装层级”（Product packaging hierarchy，来源：GS1.org），位于建立数据管理与治理政策章节中。该图绘制为四级灰色阶梯，每级阶梯上展示相应的包装插图。最上一级标为“一级包装”（PRIMARY），展示西林瓶、药瓶、泡罩包装注射器、泡罩板和无菌包装器械等单件物品；下一级“二级包装”（SECONDARY）展示装有这些物品的药盒与纸盒；第三级“二级或三级包装”（SECONDARY OR TERTIARY）展示打开的纸箱和一排盒装包装；最下一级“三级包装”（TERTIARY）展示运输箱和缠绕收缩膜的托盘箱。

narratives.en: Fig. 10, 'Product packaging hierarchy', shows four stepped shelves of packaged goods labelled, top to bottom, PRIMARY (vials, syringes, blister packs), SECONDARY, SECONDARY OR TERTIARY, and TERTIARY (cases and pallets). Source: GS1.org. Fig. 11, 'Example of packaging variations across manufacturers', shows one PRODUCT, a paracetamol 500 mg tablet, procured from two manufacturers with different pack configurations: MFR A ships 1 case of 12 packs of 50 tablets each, and MFR B ships 1 case of 10 packs of 100 tablets each.

Fig. 12, 'Mapping across product packaging hierarchy using FHIR resource'. Five record boxes, each listing identifier, description, name, characteristic and association. A GENERIC PRODUCT (identifier MR001) associates to a trade item from manufacturer A (identifier 17801415202675) and to manufacturer B's tertiary pallet (18901415202906). The pallet associates to MFR B's tertiary case (08901415202908, quantity 100), which associates to MFR B's secondary inner pack (08901415202910, quantity 50) — the packaging hierarchy expressed as chained associations.

Fig. 13, 'Transitional approach to adopting globally unique trade item numbers'. A national product code record — NPC01101001, Lamivudine 50 mg tablet, dosage form TA, route oral — branches into two tables of trade items mapped to it. The first holds GS1 GTINs (for example 58904093825793) for manufacturer MFR001 from IN, with child GTINs, child quantities of 100 and 10, 3000 eaches and a shelf life of 670. The second holds items from MFR002 from KE that have no GTIN yet and are identified only by country trade item identifiers (P006008, P006009), with child quantities of 120 and 30, 7200 eaches and a shelf life of 1095. So a national code can carry GTIN-identified and not-yet-GTIN-identified items side by side during the transition.

Fig. 14, 'Illustration of how countries can leverage WHO hosted PCMT'. Inside a panel labelled PRODUCT CATALOGUE MANAGEMENT TOOL, a GLOBAL CATALOGUE (global identifier, unit of use, pharmaceutical information such as dosage form, route of administration and strength, trade item information, and manufacturer, country of origin and shelf life) feeds COUNTRY CATALOGUE A and COUNTRY CATALOGUE B, each adding country identifiers and country-specific information such as registration numbers. The arrows are annotated 'Country catalogues to derive common product information from the global catalog'. Country A Users and Country B Users each work in their own catalogue, and the whole sits on WHO INFRASTRUCTURE.

Fig. 15, 'Illustration of how countries can share data with the WHO hosted PCMT'. It extends Fig. 14. As there, the global catalogue feeds country catalogues A and B inside the PRODUCT CATALOGUE MANAGEMENT TOOL on WHO infrastructure, used by Country A and Country B users. In addition, each country catalogue returns 'Product master data' to the global catalogue, and OTHER COUNTRIES contribute PRODUCT MASTER DATA into it from above, so the global catalogue is fed by the countries as well as feeding them.
